title: Progressive Web Apps and Service Workers
summary: A web app can keep useful features available when a connection is weak.

subtopics.title: Installable app
subtopics.explanation: A web app manifest gives the browser a name, icons, colors, and launch behavior. On supported browsers, people may add the site to a home screen. It is like a label and launch card for the app. Installation support varies, so explain the experience without promising the same prompt on every device. For example, cache versioned scripts for reuse while fetching frequently changing account data from the network. In practice, cache a versioned app shell while fetching a user’s account data fresh.

subtopics.title: Service worker
subtopics.explanation: A service worker is a script the browser can run separately from a page. It can intercept network requests and return cached files, but it does not automatically cache the whole app. It is like a helper stationed between a request and the network. Plan its lifecycle and update behavior carefully. For example, show an offline message when a user opens a route that was not cached. In practice, show an offline page when an uncached route cannot be reached.

subtopics.title: Cache strategy
subtopics.explanation: A cache strategy chooses whether a request uses the network, a saved response, or both. Use different rules for versioned assets, changing pages, and user data. It is like deciding which supplies to pack and how fresh they must be. Avoid serving private or stale data from an unsafe cache. For example, do not report a queued save as complete until the server confirms it. In practice, do not claim a queued change was saved before the server confirms it.

subtopics.title: Updates
subtopics.explanation: A new service worker can wait while older pages remain open. Version caches and remove stale entries carefully. It is like replacing a tool while people are still using the old one. Test upgrades, failed downloads, and rollback so old caches do not trap users on broken files. For example, test a service worker update while a previous page remains open. In practice, test an update while an older tab remains open.

subtopics.title: Offline experience
subtopics.explanation: Offline support should match a real user task. Explain which content is available and what must wait for a connection. Do not pretend a failed save succeeded. It is like marking a letter as sent only after it reaches the postbox. Queue actions only when conflicts and retries are handled. For example, remove old cache entries only after the new release can serve the needed files. In practice, remove obsolete cache entries without deleting assets still used by active pages.

foundations.overview: A progressive web app (PWA) uses web technologies to provide selected app-like features, such as home-screen installation or offline access. A manifest describes the app, and a service worker can manage some network requests and cached files. Think of offline support as a carefully packed travel kit: include what users need, explain what is unavailable, and never pretend an unsaved action succeeded.
foundations.whyItMatters: Offline support should solve a specific user task and communicate its limits. Cache updates and save outcomes need explicit handling to avoid stale or misleading data.
foundations.browserPerspective: Service workers are controlled by the browser and have their own update lifecycle.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Use offline support when it provides a clear user benefit and can keep data safe.
foundations.businessImpact: Installability and reliable offline workflows can help users in constrained networks.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Define cache ownership, expiration, and version cleanup.
foundations.performanceImpact: Test on a fresh install, an upgrade, and a disconnected network.
commonUseCases: Make a reference guide available during a network outage.
Provide a home-screen launch icon for a supported browser.
Cache static assets while keeping user-specific responses fresh.

commonMisconceptions.reality: Offline behavior needs deliberate caching, fallbacks, and update rules.

commonMisconceptions.myth: The service worker can safely cache all responses
commonMisconceptions.reality: Personalized or sensitive responses require strict privacy rules.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A service worker makes a site fully offline automatically.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The app must define what to cache, how to update it, and what offline tasks it supports.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Anything in Cache Storage is safe to keep indefinitely.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Stale or personal responses can create privacy and correctness risks; expire data deliberately.

keyTakeaways: A web app manifest gives the browser a name, icons, colors, and launch behavior.
A service worker is a script the browser can run separately from a page.
A cache strategy chooses whether a request uses the network, a saved response, or both.
A new service worker can wait while older pages remain open.
Offline support should match a real user task.
